subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Napoleon's Continental Blockade and Chicory Coffee
description: A fast breakdown of Napoleon's Continental Blockade and Chicory Coffee for builders.

hook.text: When Napoleon blockaded European ports in 1806, coffee imports stopped. France and Germany desperately sought substitutes.

buildup.text: Real coffee became impossibly expensive. People tried roasted barley, acorns, and figs as replacements—all terrible.

discovery.text: Chicory root—roasted and ground—became the most successful substitute. It was bitter, dark, and vaguely coffee-like.

twist.text: New Orleans still blends chicory with coffee today. The tradition came from French colonists who survived Napoleon's blockade.

climax.text: The blockade proved coffee's hold on Europe. People chose fake substitutes over abandoning the ritual.

punchline.text: No ships, no beans, roasted roots instead. War couldn't kill the coffee habit.

quiz.question: Why does New Orleans still use chicory in its coffee?
options: The tradition came from French colonists who used it during Napoleon's blockade

details.summary: Napoleon's Continental Blockade of 1806 cut Europe off from colonial imports including coffee. Desperate for a substitute, Europeans turned to roasted chicory root, which mimicked coffee's bitterness and dark color. Chicory coffee persists today in New Orleans and parts of France.
details.whyItMatters: Napoleon unintentionally created a lasting coffee alternative that survives over two centuries later, showing how political events can permanently alter food culture.
takeaways: Napoleon's blockade cut Europe off from coffee imports in 1806
Chicory root became a widely adopted coffee substitute
New Orleans and parts of France still drink chicory coffee today

faq.question: What does chicory coffee actually taste like compared to real coffee?
faq.answer: Chicory has a bitter, slightly woody flavor with caramel notes but lacks caffeine and the aromatic complexity of real coffee. When blended with coffee it adds body and reduces the amount of expensive coffee needed per pot.

faq.question: Why did New Orleans specifically adopt chicory coffee as a tradition?
faq.answer: French settlers brought the chicory habit to Louisiana, and it persisted through the Civil War when Union blockades again cut off coffee supplies. Cafe Du Monde has served chicory coffee continuously since 1862, cementing the tradition.
